title: Narrate your day
text: Describe what you are doing while changing, feeding or bathing your baby. Hearing lots of warm, back-and-forth talk is one of the strongest predictors of later language skills.

title: Tummy time, little and often
text: Start with 1–2 minutes a few times a day while your baby is awake and watched. Get down at eye level, sing, or place a mirror in front of them to make it fun.

title: Back to sleep, every sleep
text: Place your baby on their back on a firm, flat surface with no pillows, bumpers or loose blankets. Room-sharing without bed-sharing is recommended for the early months.

title: Copy the coos
text: When your baby babbles, pause and babble back. These 'serve-and-return' turns build the brain circuits for conversation.

title: Peekaboo teaches permanence
text: Hiding your face or a toy under a cloth helps babies learn that things still exist when out of sight — an important thinking milestone.

title: Offer a rainbow of foods
text: When starting solids, offer a variety of vegetables, fruits, grains and proteins. It can take 10–15 tries before a baby accepts a new taste — keep offering without pressure.

title: Name feelings out loud
text: 'You're frustrated because the tower fell.' Labelling emotions helps toddlers recognize and later manage their own feelings.

title: Read the same book again
text: Repetition is how toddlers learn. Re-reading favorites builds vocabulary and confidence; let them turn pages and point to pictures.

title: Offer two good choices
text: 'Red cup or blue cup?' Small choices give toddlers a sense of control and cut down on power struggles.

title: Anchor the door
text: Anchor dressers, TVs and bookcases to the wall. Tip-overs are a leading cause of injury for young children who love to climb.

title: Expand their sentences
text: If your child says 'big dog', reply 'Yes, a big brown dog running fast!' Expanding their words models richer language.

title: Make clean-up a game
text: Sing a tidy-up song or race a timer. Turning chores into play builds responsibility and fine-motor skills.

title: Count everything
text: Count stairs, apples, cars and spoons. Everyday counting builds early math sense far more than worksheets.

title: Pretend play is serious work
text: Playing shop, doctor or chef develops planning, empathy, language and self-control. Join in and follow your child's lead.

title: Ask open questions
text: Swap 'Did you have fun?' for 'What was the silliest thing that happened today?' Open questions spark longer conversations.

title: Practice the pause
text: Teach 'stop, breathe, think' with a simple game: freeze like a statue when the music stops. Self-control grows with practice.

title: Let them help cook
text: Washing vegetables, stirring and measuring teach math, science and new words — and kids are more likely to taste food they helped make.

title: Praise effort, not labels
text: 'You kept trying until it worked' builds persistence better than 'You're so smart'.

title: Read aloud even after they can read
text: Shared reading of books slightly above their level builds comprehension, vocabulary and connection.

title: Create a family media plan
text: Agree on screen-free zones (bedrooms, meals) and times (an hour before bed). Kids follow rules they helped write.

title: 60 minutes of movement
text: School-age children need at least an hour of active play daily. Bike rides, dancing, tag and sports all count.

title: Teach the 'trusted adults' rule
text: Help your child name at least three adults they can go to for help, and practice what to say if they feel unsafe.

title: Give an allowance with a purpose
text: Splitting money into save, spend and give jars teaches budgeting, patience and generosity.

title: Let them be bored
text: Unstructured time fuels creativity and problem-solving. Resist filling every gap with screens or activities.

title: Talk about online friends
text: Ask who they chat with in games and apps. Calm, curious conversations make kids more likely to tell you when something feels wrong.

title: Protect the sleep window
text: School-age kids need 9–12 hours. Charge devices outside the bedroom to protect sleep.

title: Prepare for puberty early
text: Start body-change conversations before they happen. Matter-of-fact, accurate information reduces anxiety.

title: Hand over a real responsibility
text: Planning a family meal, managing a pet's care or packing their own bag builds competence and independence.

title: Ten minutes of special time
text: A short daily window of undivided, child-led attention reduces attention-seeking behavior and strengthens your bond.

title: Keep the poison number handy
text: Save your local poison-control number in your phone and post it on the fridge. Store medicines and button batteries up high and locked.

title: Water safety: touch supervision
text: Young children can drown silently in seconds, even in shallow water. Stay within arm's reach near any water.

title: Model the behavior you want
text: Children copy what we do more than what we say — including how we handle stress, phones and apologies.

title: Repair after conflict
text: When you lose your temper, come back and say sorry. Repair teaches children that relationships survive mistakes.

title: Routines reduce meltdowns
text: Predictable morning and bedtime routines help children feel safe and cooperate more easily. Picture charts help younger kids.

title: Check for recalls twice a year
text: Make it a habit — when clocks change, check your car seat, crib, stroller and toys against official recall lists.

title: Keep well-child visits
text: Regular check-ups track growth and development, catch concerns early and keep vaccines on schedule.

title: Look after yourself too
text: Parental sleep, support and mental health directly affect children. Asking for help is a strength, not a failure.

title: Celebrate small wins
text: Notice and name the good moments — a kind act, a tried food, a calm bedtime. What gets noticed gets repeated.
